---
title: "Limitations and Disclosures"
---

This page lists every material limitation of the strategy and the methodology used to test it. Honest disclosure is not optional — the strategy's claim to be a defensible piece of work depends on the writeup being explicit about what it does NOT promise.

## Strategy-level limitations

### 1. Tail risk is real and bounded but not zero

Iron condor max-loss-per-spread is bounded by wing widths (5 pts SPX/RUT, 25 pts NDX, 1 pt TLT/GLD). With realistic position-sizing (1% of equity per spread), absolute drawdown in a single day is bounded. But:

- Multi-day cascade events (e.g., Volmageddon Feb 2018) can produce simultaneous emergency exits on multiple positions before the halt framework catches up.
- The wheel basket's defensive-roll mechanic (Layer 5) only triggers on fundamental criteria, not generic delta thresholds. If a name catastrophically craters between earnings cycles for fundamental reasons we don't catch, assignment + covered-call mechanics absorb the loss but don't prevent it.

### 2. Strategy capacity is limited

OptionMetrics open-interest data shows our chosen 16-delta strikes have median per-strike OI in the thousands for SPX/RUT/NDX but only dozens-to-hundreds for TLT/GLD/individual stocks. Scaling beyond ~$10–50M of capital (depending on instrument) likely encounters meaningful market-impact friction beyond what our backtest's bid-ask slippage model captures.

This is a retail / small-fund strategy, not an institutional one. The writeup reports retail-size results.

## Methodological limitations

### 3. Carr/Wu evidence base is heterogeneous across the 5-instrument cluster

Per Carr & Wu 2003/2004 Table 5: VRP is strongly empirically supported for SPX (large t-stats both raw and log forms), weaker for NDX, **not in their original 5-index sample for RUT** (we extrapolate), and **not studied for TLT or GLD** (novel application of the framework to these asset classes).

The strategy's expected edge on TLT/GLD is not anchored in the same empirical literature as SPX/NDX. Any positive findings on TLT/GLD specifically are novel and should be interpreted accordingly.

### 4. Sample-size limitations in the OOS window

Our OOS spans 2018-01-01 to 2024-12-31, ~3,500 trading days. Bollerslev/Tauchen/Zhou (2009)'s VRP-predictability sample was 1990-2007, ~17 years. Ours is 12 years and only 7 of those are out-of-sample.

Effective independent observations at the 63-day forward horizon (Head 2) ≈ 12 years × 252 / 63 = ~48 non-overlapping windows. Small. Per BTZ 2009 §3 footnote 23: "Our limited post-1990 sample prevents us from effectively studying issues having to do with longer return horizons spanning multiple years." Our sample is shorter; the same caveat applies amplified.

### 5. Daily-frequency RV components in the HAR-RV forecaster

Per BTZ 2009 §3.2.1: "Estimation of the same predictive regressions based on the traditional Black–Scholes implied variances and/or realized variances constructed from lower frequency daily data does not give rise to nearly as significant results." BTZ's preferred specification uses 5-minute intraday squared returns (78 per day plus close-to-open overnight, ~1716 per typical month).

Our wheel basket's HAR-RV forecaster (Layer 3) uses **daily** close-to-close RV components. Per BTZ, this produces weaker predictability than 5-minute intraday RV would. We do not have intraday data for the 9-name basket; documented as a known gap.

### 6. R² inflation per Boudoukh-Richardson-Whitelaw (2008)

In overlapping multi-period predictive regressions, R² inflates roughly proportionally with horizon × overlap, even in the absence of true predictability. Our 63-day forward window with daily observations creates exactly this pattern.

We mitigate by reporting **Hodrick (1992) standard errors** as the primary significance measure rather than naive Newey-West (per BTZ 2009 §3 fn21 / Ang-Bekaert 2007). R² is reported descriptively only.

### 7. Head 2 sample-size disclosure

5 labeled stress events × 63-day forward window ≤ 315 positive-class days against ~3,500 total trading days = ~9% positive base rate. The classifier learns from ~315 positives total, of which the typical fold sees ~60-180 in training. This is small. The Brier-score acceptance gate (≥5% reduction vs naive 22-day baseline) is calibrated to be informative at this sample size, but the absolute confidence in the trained model is limited by the rare-class scarcity.

### 8. Head 2 pattern coverage

The classifier is trained on 5 archetypes of regime break — vol-spike-driven sharp peaks. It can only flag breaks that *resemble* those archetypes. **Slow grinding bears (e.g., 2022-style)** and **structural-shift regimes (e.g., 2008 GFC, outside our sample)** are not in the training distribution and will not be flagged with high confidence.

### 9. American early-exercise risk on dividend-paying wheel names

Per Merton 1973 Theorem 13: American puts on dividend-paying stocks always have positive probability of premature exercise. Our wheel basket has 8 of 9 names paying dividends (only GOOGL doesn't, recently changed).

Pricing approximation: we use BS European-style for all wheel names. This **undervalues** the option for the counterparty (we underestimate the premium they'd rationally demand). Magnitude is small at our 16–25-delta OTM entry strikes; grows when underlying drops materially and put becomes ITM near ex-dividend dates.

### 10. BS pricing biases (the source of VRP itself)

Per Black & Scholes (1973) page 654 empirical test on 545 OTC option contracts: BS systematically *overvalues* options on high-variance underlyings and *undervalues* low-variance. This bias is the structural source of the volatility risk premium we harvest. We do not "out-predict" BS; we systematically take the side of the trade where empirical VRP is positive in the historical record. The strategy's edge is contingent on this bias persisting in future periods.

## Backtest limitations

### 11. Synthetic-pricing fallback when OptionMetrics IV missing

OptionMetrics has ~7-15% NaN rate on delta and IV per ticker (concentrated at deep-ITM/OTM strikes where Greeks aren't computed). Our engine falls back to BS-derived deltas using VIX/100 as ATM-IV proxy when needed. This is a known approximation; magnitude is small at our 16-delta strikes (which have populated deltas in the OptionMetrics data) but worth flagging.

### 12. Friction-model calibration is best-effort

Slippage, commission, and gap-aware-fill parameters are pre-committed but not directly calibrated to specific broker fee schedules. Real-world results will differ in these dimensions. We err conservative (more slippage in higher-VIX buckets, gap-fills at worst execution).

### 13. The v1.5 anchor is single-instrument SPX

The performance baseline we compare to (Sharpe 0.286 halts_only) is from a single-instrument SPX put-credit-spread strategy in the v1 codebase. Multi-instrument performance comparisons against this anchor are imperfect because the anchor doesn't include the call-wing or the cross-instrument diversification.

## Multiple-testing limitations

### 14. Sensitivity grid creates a multiple-testing problem

We test a 729-trial sensitivity grid (3 short-delta values × 3 spread widths × 3 DTE windows × 3 PT × 3 SL × 3 time-exit). Pure naive selection of the best-performing parameter set inflates Sharpe by selection bias.

We address this with:

- **Deflated Sharpe Ratio** (Bailey & López de Prado 2014) with **Eq. 9 implied-independent-trials correction** — N̂ = ρ̄ + (1−ρ̄)·M, where M = 729 raw trials and ρ̄ is the mean pairwise correlation across trial-return columns. The DSR uses N̂, not raw M, to avoid overstating SR̂_0.
- **Probability of Backtest Overfitting via CSCV** (Bailey/Borwein/López de Prado/Zhu 2015) with S=16. PBO is reported as a probability ∈ [0, 1] alongside DSR.

Both reported as part of every headline result. Rejection threshold: DSR (PSR) ≥ 0.95 AND PBO ≤ 0.30.

### 15. Ablation matrix creates a second multiple-testing problem

We test 6 modes (naked / halts_only / vol-regime-only / ml_only / regime+halts / full). The best-performing mode becomes the headline; others are reported for context. DSR adjusts for this N=6 multiple-testing layer.

## Live monitoring limitations

### 16. Hoeffding bound is worst-case

The bound holds for any bounded RV regardless of distribution, but it is loose. Tighter bounds exist (e.g., Bernstein, normal-approximation) for distributions where assumptions hold. We use Hoeffding for distribution-free guarantees; this means the 50/25/10% thresholds are conservative — the actual probability of regime change is at most these values, not exactly these values.

### 17. Pre-committed μ does not adapt over time

The committed μ baseline is computed from the OOS backtest and held fixed in live deployment. If we adapted μ live (e.g., updating to the rolling 12-month observed win rate), we lose the pre-commitment property and the framework becomes a moving-goalpost circular reference. Trade-off: occasional false-negatives in genuine regime changes that look "normal" relative to the pre-committed baseline.
